title: Slow Burn
full_review:
"Slow Burn" (Lionsgate), a modern-day film noir about a big-city district attorney, a beautiful assistant district attorney and a faceless criminal kingpin, tries hard to be smoky and smoldering, but ultimately fizzles.

The always compelling Ray Liotta, one of the film's executive producers, stars as District Attorney Ford Cole, a former street cop who went to law school at night and worked his way up the ladder. Self-assured and cocky, he decides to run for mayor based mostly on the strength of his conviction-getting machine, Assistant District Attorney Nora Timmer (Jolene Blalock, the Vulcan starship officer from TV's "Star Trek: Enterprise"). The only obstacle coming between Ford and the mayor's chair is mysterious (and unseen) crime boss Danny Ludin, whose shell corporations have bought all the land around a sprawling housing project that's standing in the way of his real-estate ambitions.

He has his henchmen gun down enemies, lieutenants and patsies willy-nilly. Director Wayne Beach's script, which allows lots of droning narration from Cole, includes such immortal prose as "She smelled like mashed potatoes, and every guy within 30 feet wanted to be the gravy."

The plot is set in motion by Nora's ostensibly self-defense killing of music/video-store clerk Isaac Duparde (Mekhi Phifer). The rest of the film is comprised of flashbacks, interspersed with amazingly sloppy investigative work by police and the hapless Cole. Beach includes an intriguing identity theme regarding Nora's ethnicity, but, alas, it's never developed beyond a superficial treatment.

Beach would seem to direct better than he writes, and "Slow Burn" looks quite stylish with its shiny black surfaces like anodized metal, courtesy of cinematographer Wally Pfister.

The film contains rough, crude and crass language and frank talk of rape; a sexual groping and a handful of brief sexual encounters, mostly in unrevealing close-ups except for one flash of frontal nudity; some possible rear and implied shower nudity; some nongraphic gunfire killings; and one scene of a dead body with blood.

The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian.
